steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The UK has an uncodified (unwritten) constitution: no single document sets out the rules of government. Instead, the constitution comes from: statutes (laws passed by Parliament), common law (judicial precedent), conventions (unwritten rules like the PM being an MP), and authoritative works (A.V. Dicey). This makes the constitution flexible but also less clear.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Parliamentary sovereignty: Parliament is the supreme legal authority - it can make or unmake any law. No Parliament can bind its successor. However, EU membership (1973-2020) limited sovereignty; devolution has transferred some powers; and the Human Rights Act 1998 means UK courts can declare legislation incompatible with human rights.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Devolution: the transfer of powers from Westminster to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland Act 1998: created the Scottish Parliament with powers over health, education, justice and environment (but not defence, foreign policy). Wales Act 1998/2017: Senedd Cymru has powers over health, education, some taxation. Northern Ireland Act 1998: Stormont has powers over local matters (suspended at times due to political crisis).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The West Lothian Question: Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish MPs can vote on English-only matters at Westminster, but English MPs cannot vote on devolved matters. English Votes for English Laws (EVEL) was introduced in 2015 but abolished in 2021. This remains an unresolved constitutional issue.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Explain what is meant by an uncodified constitution and evaluate whether the UK should adopt a codified constitution. | Q: Describe how devolution works in the UK and assess its impact on UK governance. | Q: Evaluate whether parliamentary sovereignty is still meaningful in the modern UK.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: UK constitution = UNCODIFIED (statutes + common law + conventions). Flexible but unclear. Devolution: Scotland, Wales, NI have their own parliaments/assemblies with LIMITED powers. Westminster retains defence, foreign policy. Parliamentary sovereignty: still exists in LAW but limited in PRACTICE by devolution, human rights, international agreements.
